speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend whether my motion is in any way preventing him from saying anything that he desires on the motion of the Minister of Justice?

No. I am explaining my point that the motion this afternoon of the right hon. leader of the government prevents all kinds of amendments being moved. The right hon. Prime Minister said so in so many words.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is something quite different from what my hon. friend just said. What my hon. friend implied was that I had been seeking to prevent hon. members from discussing this motion.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The motion before the Chair.

No, but it reminds me of a similar motion that was made by Mr. Northrup, the effect of which was to prevent Sir

Wilfrid Laurier from exposing his views on the motion made by Sir Robert Borden. I do not say that the motion made by the Prime Minister this afternoon has the effect of preventing discussion on the main motion, but here is the point to which I am coming. The motion of the Prime Minister, according to his own words, according to his own interpretation and according to the rules of the house prevents any kind of amendment; yes, prevents all kinds of amendments which might come within the four corners of the resolution and which might help to remove certain apprehensions that exist and help to prevent certain injustices that otherwise are going to follow. I do not say that the right hon. the Prime Minister made his motion to prevent me from moving my amendment. He did not know about it. Nobody knew about it. The amendment I intended to move is within the four corners of the resolution. The reason advanced by the Prime Minister for making his motion, to move the previous question, was to avoid all kinds of discussion outside the four corners of the resolution-that is the reason he gave-to avoid amendments that he had heard somebody was going to move and which might set the house afire. The amendment which I had in mind to propose and which I am going to read before sitting down was within the iowf corners of tbr resolution and would have prevented an injust treatment being imposed to a province in particular by the passing of the measure as it is at present drafted.
We have been told this afternoon that the populations of certain provinces have been reduced by reason of the war. But no evidence has been produced of that; no indication has been given of the truth of that statement. So far as the house is concerned, we do not know. But if we look upon certain documents that are at our disposal, we come to the conclusion that the decrease in the population of Saskatchewan started in 1931 and continued to decrease until 1936. There was no war on then, but the population of the province decreased considerably from 1931 to 1936. I am not quite correct in saying that. My information is taken from a report I have of the live births for all the provinces of Canada. If hon. gentlemen will look at that report they will see that the birth-rate in Canada has been increasing, with the exception of in two provinces, and one in particular, the birth-rate has been very rapidly decreasing between 1931 and 1936. That was in Saskatchewan.
I hope that nobody will accuse me of making any plea that would be prejudicial to the fair and just interests of the province of Saskatchewan. If there is an agreement that should be

Redistribution
made to protect the province of Saskatchewan, which has suffered so much from drought, let us make it. But let us do something for the other provinces also in order to compensate for the advantages so given to one province at the expense of the others. That is my proposal.
I would have been ready to consider favourably any request to help maintain at a proper number the representation of Saskatchewan in this parliament. I know that that province has been through difficult days, that it has experienced hard times. I am ready to consider that and to provide some relief, if I may use the word, in reference to representation in the House of Commons. But I think that something else should be done to compensate the other provinces that have been receiving no consideration in any redistribution made in consequence of the decennial censuses that we have had since 1871.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Before my hon. friend proceeds any further, on a point of order, I was not in a position to say at the moment whether he was correct when he made the statement that the motion which was moved by Mr. Northrop was the same as the one I moved to-day. I have since had an opportunity to look into the matter, and I wish now to say that the motion moved by Mr. Northrop was not the same as I moved to-day. I wish to make that quite clear to my hon. friend. If he wishes to have the facts verified, he will find the motion Mr. Northrop moved set out in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, 1943, citation 215:
On the 9th of April, 1913, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Hr. Hazen rose at the same time and Mr. Northrop moved that Mr. Hazen "be now heard."

Technically there is something in the point raised by the Prime Minister. I shortened my recital, but the effect of the two motions is just the same. Mr. Northrop moved that Sir Douglas Hazen be given the right of way, the right to speak in place of Sir Wilfrid Laurier who had risen at the same time. The speaker had "seen" Sir Wilfrid Laurier first and authorized him to speak, when Mr. Northrop rose and moved according to the roles of the house that Sir Douglas Hazen be "seen" by the Speaker and be allowed to speak. A vote was taken, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Liberals were defeated. Sir Wilfrid Laurier had- to sit down and Sir Douglas Hazen rose in his place and moved a motion like the one the Prime Minister has moved. He moved the previous question, without making any speech at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend has not had to sit down, nor has he been prevented from uttering any word he wished to say.

No, but that is not exactly representing my position. I am referring to a situation in years gone by similar to the one we are facing to-day. When a motion was moved preventing any amendment, just as the Prime Minister's motion does to-day, I can speak on the main motion; yes, other members have been speaking on it and others will speak, but there can be no amendment moved even to better the resolution that is before the house, after the previous question has been moved. That is my criticism. It prevents all members of the house from any section of the country from moving any amendment that would improve the text of the resolution which we are at present considering and which might help to dispel the anxiety which exists in many quarters and prevent at least the injustice that is being done to certain partners to the pact of confederation, an injustice that may remain on our statute books until ,1951 after the next decennial census is taken.
The amendment, Mr. Speaker, which I had in mind to move was very short. I was simply suggesting to add to paragraph 1 of the proposed measure to be introduced in the British house the following words:
However, a readjustment of the representation of the provinces in the House of Commons in consequence of the aforesaid decennial census shall be made previous to the holding of a general election.
I wanted to avoid the holding of a general election on a redistribution which was made after the decennial census of 1931. If there is an election before 1945 and the war is not then concluded, that election will be fought on a representation based on the decennial census of 1931.

No, 1931, because it is not proposed to deal with redistribution based on 1941 census until after the war. The proposal is to postpone until then the redistribution based on the decennial census of 1941. So that, if we have an election before the war is concluded, that election will have to be fought on a redistribution made after the decennial census of 1931. That I regard as an injustice.
If we had embodied in the amendment to the constitution that in the event of a general election before the conclusion of the term of office of this parliament redistribution would previously be made in consequence of the
Redistribution

1941 census, no province would have had cause to complain. Some attention could then be given to the province of Quebec, which representation now seems to be fixed at sixty-five for the rest of the life of Canada. Attention could also be given to the maritime provinces representation. I suggest it would have been fair to amend the resolution in that way. Such amehdment would not have brought in any question or any subject not within the principle of the resolution.
Even if we are deprived of the right of making an amendment to have that situation cleared up, I wonder if it will be possible to obtain from the Prime Minister an understanding that before we go to the people some arrangement will be made regarding redistribution in order that no province will suffer from the results of the amendment to the constitution which is proposed. But we have not even that. All that is proposed now is to postpone the redistribution, but we are not told what is to be done in the meantime.
The redistribution is postponed on account of the war; but there is a possibility that the war will not be an obstacle to the holding of a general election. The government is afraid of dealing in the House of Commons now with the problem of redistribution on account of difficulties which may exist, of troubles which may be raised, of representations which may be made by certain provinces and controversies which might endanger the unity of this country. Yet the government does not seem to be afraid of plunging Canada into a general election during the war and before redistribution has been made. That is the situation.
All the arguments which have been advanced up to the present against redistribution apply with a hundred times more force to the holding of a general election before the war is over, but we have not a word as to that. They will postpone redistribution and wait for the opportunity of calling a general election later on, and that general election will be held on the basis of the decennial census of 1931.
I repeat that this is not justice; it is not fair treatment. There is certainly a possibility, between understanding citizens of Canada who have in the past faced many difficulties, of reaching an agreement which will not sow any prejudice or create any disunity in the country. Speaking for my province particularly, I say there would be no trouble there, because there was none in the past when the number of our representatives remained at sixty-five and representation changed in other sections of Canada.

Of course we have difficulties; we have misunderstandings; but what country under the face of the sun is without difficulties? One has only to listen to what is being said in the parliament of South Africa, in the parliament of Australia, even in the parliament of England, to know that they are not afraid there to discuss the problems of the day and that they do not shelve them indefinitely.
It would have been possible, I repeat, to deal with this problem and to grant relief, if necessary, to -the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba according to circumstances and evidence placed before the House of Commons. That case is not made now. If we would deal with redistribution, the case could be made on figures, not on words, not on suppositions; and afterwards it would be easy to reach an understanding. I can guarantee that no trouble would be raised in my province against an equitable arrangement equally fair to all the members of the pact of confederation.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, it is with a deep feeling of regret and sorrow that I rise in my place to-day. The first reason is that, according to the press of the province of Quebec, not long ago, on June 22, it was unanimously resolved by the Quebec legislature to send a protest to the dominion government regarding precisely the motion which is now before us. It is very seldom, sir, that there is such unanimity of opposing groups; but this time Conservatives and Liberals, English and French-speaking Canadians and even Jews in the Quebec legislature united to send a solemn protest to this government against such a move as is now contemplated. It is wrong, of course, to represent Quebec as a province composed wholly of French-speaking Canadians. There is a large number of Englishspeaking Canadians, of people of all origins and of all religions in the province of Quebec. Jews have been elected to the Quebec legislature; in fact the first Jew who was elected to the legislative assembly of any part of the British empire, even before Disraeli was elected in London, was a Jew named Hart, who was elected in the French-Canadian constituency of Three Rivers. Therefore we cannot overlook the fact that the unanimity of Quebec on this matter is not only that of French-speaking Canadians but that of all those who live within the boundaries of that province, who are represented by members of different religious faiths and of different languages, residing within its precincts. That is why I am so surprised, in fact dumbfounded, that

Redistribution
the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) have not tabled a copy of that solemn protest, which was not a private letter, because, as I have been credibly informed, it was an official letter of the Quebec government to the dominion government protesting in clear terms against such a move.
We live under a constitution that was passed by Westminster after lengthy discussion in Quebec and in Charlottetown; it is that constitution that we must respect if we are to have order and good government in this country; and if anyone says anything disparaging of that constitution, anything that brings it into disrepute in the minds of his fellow citizens, he is doing something that is contrary to the defence regulations.
The remarks that have been made by the Minister of Justice, who is a distinguished member of the bar, have greatly surprised me. He spoke of extraneous subjects and thereby invited discussion on a most controversial matter. He gave me the impression of a man pouring oil on the fire. I would have understood his position if immediately before he had risen, someone had discussed language and religious matters relating to the subject before us. But no one did so. He was the first to speak on the matter, and he himself indicated that such cases as he referred to were mentioned only by few people and were not important. A minister who holds such a rank in the government of the country had no right on such a solemn occasion to bring forward such matters, adding straw to the fire, in fact lighting the fire of prejudice throughout the country.
I am a much older member than the hon. gentleman. I have been here nearly twenty years and he is a newcomer. But never have I raised the question of race and religion in this house, and I have good friends among members who are staunch imperialists, who have not my religious faith and who do not speak my language. But I believe that we can come easily to an understanding-on what basis? On the basis of fairness. And so long as a minister admits that there is unfairness somewhere, unfairness in this act, in the way it has been interpreted and applied, whether in my province or in a sister province, the first thing to do, if we are to have national unity, is to remedy that injustice and to have the courage to do so. So long as injustice is admitted it is the duty of the government to correct it, and the government cannot come and say that because we are at war they will not correct that injustice. That is cowardice; it is not
worthy of men of the character and determination of those who sit on the treasury benches.
I do not admit that in times of war unfairness should be cherished at the expense of fairness. I do not admit that, and no member will admit it. The Minister of Justice cannot enunciate the principle that in time of war unfairness shall subsist because there might be criticism in some quarters. No member can rise in his place and defend such a theory. How is it that the Minister of Justice, who is the guardian of the law, rose in his place and made a speech in which he said that we do not want to invite controversy, while at the same time he invited controversy, invited prejudice, invited hatred and religious fights and struggles in this country? 1 cannot conceive it, and I tell you, sir, it is a very dangerous thing to deal with. It is a very dangerous matter to handle. I saw that some of his colleagues here were worrying while he was giving his explanation. What has the question of language to do with redistribution in this country? What has the matter of religion to do with redistribution?
Members of this house who belong to the army may suffer an injustice, it is said. As the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres pointed out, is there one member of this house who would do injustice to anyone in the armed forces, whether overseas or in this country? No one would do that; no one would agree to a proposal which my hon. friend could not make but did mention, about members of the armed forces belonging to our house being given the same seats. No one would object to that even if those members were not here. No member would think of objecting to that. Therefore, why use such an argument in regard to such a question? Why raise the patriotic issue, waving that flag that we have not? What is patriotism, sir? It is a simple thing. It is love of our country and respect for our institutions.
What is the motto of French Canadians? It is, "Our religion, our tongue and our rights". That may be the motto of English-speaking Canadians as well. But because the French Canadian speaks French and the English Canadian speaks English, or because the Scottish Canadian speaks Gaelic, that is no reason why we cannot come to an understanding, provided that understanding is based on fairness. And in this case the Minister of Justice has admitted that there is something wrong, something which should be righted by the government-until lately. Why did the Prime Minister state in this house in words that were very clear, words that were not
Redistribution

obscure, that since the question of redistribution had been mentioned in the speech from the throne the government would proceed with it at this session, before the expiration of the session? AVhat happened between the time when the Prime Minister made that statement and the moment when this resolution appeared on the order paper? What was the reason for the change? How is it that no one doubted all along that before the expiration of the session the government would deal with the question of redistribution? I cannot understand it and nobody can. It is a mystery.
Coming to the resolution itself and the way in which it is drafted, I have a few words to say; but before doing so I would again ask the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice to table a copy of the solemn protest received from the Quebec government, not only on behalf of the French-speaking Canadians of Quebec, but on behalf of those people of Quebec whom they represent, whatever may be their race or religion.
In regard to the resolution I have a correction to make in the quotation of Doctor Skelton by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party. Doctor Skelton appearing before the committee said that Canada was the only country in the world that could not amend its constitution. It is true, and it is not true. All dominions, with the exception of Canada, have the right to amend their own constitution. They were all subject to disallowance by the British government, as we are now. Therefore, what was the use of having power to amend the constitution when, on the other hand, the British government had the power of disallowance of any act passed by any such parliament of the dominions. An exception could be made with respect to Ireland, in these later years. But it is the only dominion where there is no right of disallowance. Therefore Doctor Skelton gave a superficial view of the constitutions of other dominions.
Now, to come to this resolution, the government of Canada proposes to go to the British government asking for an amendment of the constitution with respect to the holding of a redistribution. As one who at the request of the late Minister of Justice made a report on redistribution in each county of Quebec, covering the last eighty years, and who prepared a booklet used by that right hon. gentleman as well as by the hon. member for Rich-elieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) when they discussed the matter with Conservative ministers at that time, I believe I have the right to protest against a move like this. I have also the right to protest against the way in which the resolution has been drafted.

The other day while speaking, not about the British government but about His Majesty the King and Her Majesty the Queen, I said I did not feel humble when speaking to them, through you, sir. I did not feel humble, although I do feel so at times. I did not feel humble, because I represent people I am proud of, and I believe that is the feeling of all hon. members elected for the various constituencies of this country. But I do not see the government of Canada, which is supposed to be on an equal footing with the British government, going humbly before the lords spiritual and temporal asking them to amend the constitution. I do not see them going humbly

and the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) repeated that expression at the beginning of his speech-going humbly like the burgher of Calais, or like one of our colleagues who had to act humbly, and who had to repeat flectamus qenua four times the other day before his withdrawal w-as accepted. I cannot agree with that. I cannot agree with it because I think we should have the dignity of an autonomous country within the empire. We should have the right to amend our constitution ourselves, as has been said so well by some hon. members. I do not see how we can go twice a year, or once a year to London to ask for an amendment to our constitution. What is our constitution worth, if it has to be changed like that every year? I admit that nothing is perfect in the constitution. But when Mr. Bennett stated that the constitution should be amended I asked him very often, "What part of the constitution do you wish to amend?" He could not answer me.
Last year the constitution was amended to permit the introduction of an unemployment measure. This year it will be amended to destroy a vital part of the British North America Act, a part which deals with representation in the House of Commons, the representation of a group of men who must have their say in our deliberations, and who must have no fear or favour in the conduct of their discussion. That is the British North America Act. Every province agreed to the constitution at the time of confederation. The government has no power to go to London to ask for a change without at least asking the people what they think of it. It should ask the people by way of a. plebiscite, the fashion of which was begun last year.
This matter affects not only the dominion. It affects the provinces, and affects every citizen in the country. Therefore each province and each citizen, each man and woman have the right to express their views on the matter. If this motion is passed I hope the government will be fair enough to attach to it

Redistribution
a copy of the solemn protest received from the government of Quebec against such a change before an election. The suggestion of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres is only fair and just. He did not offer an amendment, because he could not, on account of the Prime Minister's motion. But does it not appeal to every hon. member that it would be only fair that the next election should be conducted after the last census, and not the census before the last one. What is the purpose of a census? It is to establish a basis of representation in accordance with the provisions of the British North America Act. What is the use of spending a million dollars for a census, if it is of no use, and if it does not serve the purpose for which it is made?
There is no question of any intervention by Mr. Anthony Eden in respect of the matter of redistribution, except that if the matter is taken to Westminster he will be one who will have to help decide. The same applies to Lord Halifax. What has Lord Halifax to do with this matter? What has Mr. Anthony Eden to do with this matter? He may have something to do with it when the resolution is over there, but only at that time.
To this moment no one has explained satisfactorily to me the reason for the sudden change of the government in connection with this matter. I do not know the reason. I took some notes of what the Minister of Justice said, and he made one observation which astounded me. This is a proposal for a modification of the act of 1867. I do not know if my understanding of his statement was correct, but if it is not, he will no doubt correct me. When a change is to be made in the British North America Act those concerned must deal with a constitution formulated by the fathers of confederation to weld into one nation two groups of peoples of different origin and with different religions. That is not the question. It is admitted that different people have different religions. But I say that although they do not belong to the same race, or do not have the same religious beliefs, or are not of the same origin, still we are all in the same boat and we have to make the best of it. Therefore it is not by leaving an injustice, and permitting it to continue that we are going to bring about a greater degree of peace and unity in Canada.
I have said it before, and I now repeat that it is a great mistake to consider French Canadians of the same class and in the same walk of life as being different mentally from English, Scotch or Irish citizens performing the same work. That is a great mistake. All have the same interests. They are fellow *citizens. They must work in unison, and they
will do so, provided no one raises the cry of prejudice or brings before their eyes matters which may be exploited by a few individuals unworthy of the name Canadian.
I was sorry that the Minister of Justice took the trouble to bring that matter before the house. Some of his statements were commendable, but they would have been just as good on another occasion. But this was not the time to say what he said because, as was pointed out by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon)-and rightly so-what he said was irrelevant.
The matter before the house is one of representation of people within the boundaries of a certain unit known as a constituency. All those people have the right to be represented in the House of Commons, and it would be an injustice both to French Canadians of Ontario as well as to English-speaking citizens of Quebec not to proceed with redistribution according to the solemn promise which was made in the speech from the throne, and which was repeated not long ago by the Prime Minister. I see no reason for it.
What explanation have we been given? The hon. member who preceded me in the debate suggested that this was being done to have more seats for Quebec in the next election. No, sir; that will not work. Even Englishspeaking Canadians in Canada would not agree to any injustice to both English-speaking and French-speaking citizens, which would have the effect of greater support for the choice of the government in any constituency. I believe that the French-speaking people and the English-speaking people in this country are fair-minded. The only trouble is that they have not been told the things that they should have been told; they have not been spoken to in the language that should have been used. But when they read Hansard they will see the admission made by the Minister of Justice that there was something wrong, that there was, to use the expression of my hon. friend who spoke previously, a nigger in the wood-pile. They will want to know what the nigger in the wood-pile is. If they proceed farther, they will see that the Minister of Justice has admitted that there is something wrong somewhere, that we must wait until the end of the war to do something and not create a disturbance.
Our soldiers are fighting for freedom and liberty, and yet an injustice exists in our midst. Is it possible to conceive that while we are trying to cure the evils of the world, we allow them to exist in our midst? That is my last word. I make a special appeal to the Prime Minister; I make a special appeal
Redistribution

to the Minister of Justice; I ask them in the interests of all Canadians to conceive it to be their duty to drop the motion for the previous question and the motion before the chair.

Mr. Speaker, after listening this afternoon to the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent), I concluded that the consent of the provincial governments or legislatures had not been obtained to the amendment to the British North America Act proposed by this resolution. If I am not correct in that conclusion, the Minister of Justice can correct me. If I am correct, I think some explanation is due to the members of this house and to the country as to why this consent was not obtained. All the provinces are interested, and in my opinion they should have been consulted. Before an amendment was made to the British North America Act to establish a system of unemployment insurance, the consent of the provinces was obtained. But nothing of that kind has been done on this occasion.
I do not think this is the proper time to have redistribution; I do not think it would be fair to some of the western provinces, but I rise this evening to place myself on record as being opposed to any amendment to the British North America Act unless the provincial legislatures have agreed to such amendment. Any amendment to the British North America Act should involve the approval of the legislature of -each province. I intend to support the resolution, but I do so upon the understanding that it creates no precedent as far as further amendments to the British North America Act are concerned.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution we are requested to pass does not meet with my approval and I must admit frankly that I cannot countenance it. Here are my reasons. In 1867 the British North America Act fixed at 65 the number of members for the province of Quebec. Besides, the same legislation states that the other provinces will be entitled to as many constituencies as the number of times their population is divisible by one sixty-fifth of that of the province of Quebec.
This clause was included in the Confederation pact in order to safeguard the rights of Quebec as compared to the other provinces and ensure that it would be fairly represented in Parliament. If the population of Quebec should increase more rapidly than that of the other provinces in a ten-year period, it may

well be that the representation of these be decreased, as on the contrary, it may increase if the population of Quebec should experience an appreciable decrease.
The British North America Act specifies that the representation shall be adjusted following every tenth-year census. A census has been taken in 1941; according to the constitution the readjustment of representation should take place before the next general election.
However, the government, in the resolution now before the house, request that this readjustment be postponed until after the end of the war. As main arguments in favour of its resolution the government state that we are at war and that such a readjustment in war-time would inevitably cause dissension.
I still believe, Mr. Speaker, that the war should not be an excuse or a pretext for the establishment of a precedent or for any abuse. Time and again, I have protested in this house against the tendency of the government, under pretext of the state of war, to alter or amend our parliamentary set-up. The readjustment is to be made following the census taken every ten years. It has been taken during the war. Why have not the government, at that time, thought of postponing it? Since the census has been taken why should the readjustment of representation be postponed?' It had been announced in the speech from the throne, on January 28. On May 14th last the Right Hon. Prime Minister informed the house that this measure would be brought down in the course of the present session. Exactly a month later, the Right Hon. Prime Minister announced the intention of the government of having the constitution amended so as to postpone until the end of the wrar the readjustment of representation. Why this change in policy?
Any amendment to the constitution would establish a dangerous precedent, even in wartime. Besides, the constitution should be amended only in cases of absolute necessity. Furthermore, the readjustment of representation bill does not affect our war effort, either directly or indirectly, but is purely and simply an administrative affair.
The government fear that this readjustment may cause serious dissensions. This could not possibly be the case in Quebec, for that province may have neither more nor less than 65 constituencies. The protests could be based only on the alteration of the boundaries of existing constituencies and the government could, very wisely, avoid these, for reasons of war emergency. On account of

Redistribution
the increase in the population of the province of Quebec, the prairie provinces will lose seven or eight electoral districts. I under-[DOT] stand that if the redistribution was to be done at once, some hon. members, and especially those who sit on the other side of the house, would rise in protest. What happens is solely due to the constitution. The population of Quebec, a province where large families are the rule, which is no commonplace title to fame, has materially increased since the last ten years, and many persons who have left other provinces have found that Quebec was hospitable. Such are the facts. The province of Quebec is justified in demanding that the constitution be upheld, especially since the latter is the very basis of our representative system. Speaking in the Quebec house, whose members were unanimous on that point, Prime Minister Godbout has demanded on behalf and for the protection of the province of Quebec a representation wholly in accordance with the constitution. That desire on the part of the provincial government, and it is also the desire of the whole population of the province, cannot and must not be ignored.
The resolution clearly emphasizes that the readjustment of representation will be proceeded with at the first session held after the cessation of hostilities. The question comes up:	What will happen if the war is to last
one, two or three years longer, or if there is a general election before the cessation of hostilities? If the resolution is passed and if the government should decide to hold a general election in the coming fall or next winter, it follows that the number of constituencies will still be 245 while it should, in fact, be only 237 or 238.
Do you not believe, Mr. Speaker, that an injustice is being done as regards the rights which the province of Quebec enjoys under the confederation agreement, and that, under the pretext of war, the democratic character of our parliamentary system is being set aside? In my opinion to postpone the redistribution is simply to check the influence which Quebec is entitled to have on the political destinies of this country.
The Prime Minister has referred to an unusual movement, of population between the various provinces as a result of the enforcement of the mobilization act and the opening of war plants. The argument is not absolutely convincing, since it is quite possible that the situation may, with the cessation of hostilities, become both normal and permanent.
I am opposed to this resolution for the reasons which I have just stated. I consider that I have no right to take any other stand;
a principle is involved, and it is also a matter of justice for my province. Besides, this resolution interferes with the constitution and my province is especially affected. The government has no justification for overriding the constitution.
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): Mr. Speaker, there is very little I think it is necessary for me to say at this time. I wish, however, to deal with one objection that was featured rather prominently in the speeches that have been made.
First of all, it would appear that there are many members of this house who feel it is proper that redistribution should be postponed. They also realize that this cannot be done without some legislation which would be operative notwithstanding the ordinary provisions of the British North America Act. Legislation that would operate notwithstanding the terms of the British North America Act could not be passed in this country and must be obtained from the parliament of the United Kingdom. It has even been suggested; that the old traditional form of "a humble address may be presented to His Majesty" indicates a degree of humility that is not compatible with the autonomous state of this country. I do not think that in the courteous forms which have been handed down to us there is anything that need prove a serious danger to our autonomy. But it is a fact that the only way in which legislative provision can be obtained that would operate notwithstanding the provisions of the British North America Act is by an act enacted by the parliament of the United Kingdom. I trust it will not always be so. I trust that there will be a system devised whereby it will be possible for us to deal here in our country with the problems which concern us. But the establishment of that system will require an amendment to be made to the British North America Act, and that amendment will have to be made by the parliament of the United Kingdom. I do not think it would be the temper of this parliament at the present time to undertake to establish any permanent system for amending in a permanent fashion the provisions of our constitution. I hope that day will arrive and that it will arrive soon enough for me to witness a system found and made operative whereby things like this will not require even to be registered, for that is really what it amounts to, as the statute of another parliament.
When it comes to making amendments to our constitution I would like to suggest to hon. members that there appears to be a fundamental distinction to be observed. Confederation was not really a pact between provinces.
Redistribution

As a matter of fact, there was only one province of the United Canadas, Upper and Lower, at the time confederation came into existence. But it was nevertheless the system worked out by responsible prominent leaders of the population of the areas which then, constituted, on the one hand, the united province of Upper and Lower Canada, and- on the other hand the maritime provinces, and it was provided that under this system provincial legislatures and provincial governments would be established to deal with certain matters over which they were allocated exclusive jurisdiction. The courts have held that the provinces in the exercise of jurisdiction in the field allocated to them are sovereign states.
There are other matters which were not so allocated for administrative purposes to provincial legislatures or to provincial governments, but which were either expressly allocated to the federal parliament or which come under the residual clause under which parliament is competent to deal with them.
I would readily concede to hon. members that if there were to be any suggested amendment to change the allocation of legislative or administrative jurisdiction as between the provinces, on the one hand, and the federal parliament, on the other, it could not properly [DOT]be done without the consent of the organism that was set up by the constitution to have powers that would assumedly be taken from that organism.
Apart from the matters that are expressly allocated to the provincial legislatures and provincial governments, there are other matters which the representatives of the inhabitants of the provinces who sit in this parliament are the competent persons to deal with, and here in this instance is something having to do with representation in this house. That is something which is not allocated to the provincial legislatures or to the provincial governments. That is something which interests the inhabitants of the provinces, but the inhabitants of the provinces as electors have sent representatives to this national parliament to represent them, and I suggest that when dealing with matters in that category the members elected by the people of the provinces, who are also the people of Canada, are those who have to take their responsibility in determining whether they are in the interests of Canada or otherwise.
The example that was given by the hon. member is a case where it was eminently proper that the consent of the legislatures be obtained because it meant transferring to this parliament jurisdiction which in 1867 had been allocated to those legislatures. I submit

that it would have been quite improper to take away from the provinces without their consent anything that they had by the constitution. That, I think, Mr. Speaker, disposes of the objection founded on the protest of the Quebec government or the Quebec legislature. They may have expressed their opinion, but in respect of matters concerning representation in this house they are merely electors, and they are represented here by members of parliament who have been elected by them and by the other electors of the respective constituencies in which they have their homes.
As to the amendment which the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) would have liked to move, may I point out that the hon. member must have overlooked the terms of paragraph 5 of section 51 of the British North America Act; he would expressly provide that there would not be an election until redistribution shall have taken place. Well, the constitution provides that any readjustment, whenever made, is not operative until the dissolution of the parliament under which it is made. Paragraph 5, section 51, states:
Such readjustment shall not take effect until the termination of the then existing parliament.
So that a bill with that kind of amendment added to it would have been without any effect at all. It would merely have meant that a redistribution might be made at one session instead of at another session of the same parliament. There is no amendment to the constitution necessary to do that. I was not here at the time, but I am told that the redistribution following the census of 1931 was not made until the second session following the publication of the census reports. There would not only be this fact that it would utterly destroj' whatever effect this bill in the resolution provides for, but it seems to me that there are also two serious constitutional objections to the hon. member's proposals.
One would be to deprive the crown of its right to dissolve parliament until there had been a session where redistribution had been enacted; and the other-an indirect effect at that-would have been to make this parliament almost eternal, to prolong the life of this parliament until the majority saw fit to enact a provision for redistribution. There would have been no obligation to enact it at any special time, and if the majority of this parliament continued session after session- to find itself unable to agree on a redistribution the life of the parliament would be automatically prolonged by the terms of the amendment thus introduced.

Redistribution

Will the minister permit a question?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Certainly.

When this resolution is adopted and when the bill is passed by the British House of Commons postponing redistribution until after the war, supposing the war concludes in 1946 or 1947; does the hon. minister contend that we could not have a general election at the expiration of this parliament, which expires in 1945?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am not contending anything of the kind. What I am contending is that if an amendment such as that suggested by the hon. member were made, it would not be possible to have a dissolution until after a redistribution had been agreed to by parliament.
Hon. members have asked, what has happened between the speech from the throne, in which redistribution was announced, and the introduction of this resolution? What happened was that figures collected during the last census became available, and upon looking at them it was realized that what they would mean, with a redistribution at this time, was a situation as exposed to the house-this afternoon, and it was felt that that would not be fair. Now it is submitted with great vehemence that when anything unfair exists it should be corrected. That may be so, but I submit that the agreement on the extent to which there is unfairness would not be sufficiently unanimous to warrant provoking a debate or debates upon it at the present time.
For these reasons, although I agree with hon. members that it would have been preferable if the result desired could be achieved in some other way than by asking a parliament outside of this country to pass a statute, since that is not possible, and since the object pursued seems to be desirable, I submit that the resolution should meet with the concurrence of the members of the house.
The question is on the main motion. Shall the motion carry?
On division.
The same division.

The same division.
Motion (Mr. St. Laurent) agreed, to.

I was paired with the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruick-shank). Had I voted I would have voted against the resolution.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, July 1, consideration in commitee of a resolution to grant to his majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
Freight assistance on western feed grains,

The other night some reference was made to dehydration, and the minister told the hon. member for Fraser Valley that he would make a statement on the question under one of these items. Under which of the items will he make that statement?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
What I did say to the hon. member for Fraser Valley was that I would be prepared to answer his question on this item. I am not sure what the question was, but I presume it had to do with the dehydration plant in British Columbia. I have an answer with regard to the plant at Haney. British Columbia. If the Haney plant can be fully and properly equipped for the dehydration of potatoes and can manufacture a product which will meet the board's specifications, and if the wartime prices and trade board will approve the production of additional dehydrated potatoes from British Columbia, the board may give the Haney plant a contract for a small quantity of dehydrated potatoes in 1943-possibly 200 tons. That is the statement which I have had prepared to answer l Mr. Durocher.]
the question in regard to that plant. However, I am not sure that that was the question intended.

As the hon. member for Fraser Valley and I are both interested in this matter, and as the hon. member for Fraser Valley had to leave the chamber a few moments ago, perhaps the minister would not mind answering a question of mine, because both of us have been appealed to. This is a plant which has been in business in the town of Haney for a considerable time. Some assurance must have been given to the management of the plant that they would be given an order for dehydrating potatoes, because before I left the district at Easter time one of the prominent farmers in the district told me he had contracted his potatoes to this plant. My understanding was that many farmers both in the Fraser Valley and New' Westminster constituencies had agreed to sell their potatoes to the plant.
Since that time and up until the present the management of the plant has been endeavouring to obtain a contract from the wartime prices and trade board, or whatever board has to do w'ith it, to supply dehydrated potatoes. My information to-day is that it is without success. An argument was used that the Fraser valley was known as a deficiency area, in so far as potatoes are concerned. May I say that I absolutely disagree with that finding? In fact, I cannot understand how such a finding could have been given, because I myself remember not so very long ago-just prior to the war-hundreds of tons of potatoes being allowed to rot in the Fraser valley. And the reason why potatoes have not been grown, particularly in the Fraser valley, to any great extent, is that the price did not warrant production, or did not cover the cost of production. But the fact is that the Fraser valley is a splendid district for the growing of potatoes.
I tell the minister and the committee now that I take strong exception to the statement made by the member of the wartime prices and trade board that potatoes growm in the Fraser valley were not very good. I do not know what potatoes he was talking about, but he certainly was not talking about potatoes grown in the Fraser valley. I can tell you, Mr. Chairman, and members of this committee, that potatoes have been dished up in this city that we would not feed to the hogs, let alone to human beings.
I resent very much the statement made by that member of the board that there were no good potatoes grown in the Fraser valley. And, in so far as any deficiency area is concerned, it is not correct to make that state-

War Appropriation-Agriculture
ment, because we did grow potatoes in past years. I have seen hundreds of tons going to waste. I am going to ask the minister why this firm cannot get a contract for the dehydration of potatoes. The opinion is that there will be an excess of potatoes grown in the Fraser valley, that there will be at least 15,000 tons more this year than were grown last year.
It seems strange to me; if there is anything against the plant or the management we should know about it. The excuse cannot be given that they have not potatoes, or that the potatoes are not good. I would ask the minister to tell us why this firm *cannot obtain a contract for dehydrating potatoes.

The wartime agricultural supplies board has no information as to whether the Berryland plant at Haney, British Columbia, has pre-processing equipment such as pealers, cutters, dicers and plungers, or whether this plant is equipped for that work. Our representative at the Summerland experimental station, Mr. Atkinson, advised Mr. J. M. Armstrong recently, namely on June 23, that the Haney plant ordered temperature control equipment for their plant, and that they have no information yet that the order can be filled, or that the equipment can be supplied. Mr. Atkinson has informed Mr. Armstrong, or did inform him, in the Lethbridge area in June, that he believed that the dehydrator and the layout of the plant was satisfactory. That statement has been made.
That it was satisfactory?

Yes, that he believed it was. But we have no absolute information with regard to it. We have no definite information in regard to it. That is the first matter that has to be cleared up, namely, whether the plant is properly equipped to do the job, if the contract is given.
The second point is this: the price to be paid by the special products board for dehydrated potatoes in 1943 was thirty-five cents per dried pound. That is what is asked. That is higher than will be paid in Alberta, the price there being thirty-three cents, and prices in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick being thirty-three and thirty-two cents respectively. The price for Prince Edward Island is not known, but it is presumed it will be thirty-two cents. Only in Ontario, where a relatively small quantity of potatoes have been contracted for, will the price be as high as British Columbia. So that there is the question as to whether we can get dehydrated potatoes at a lower price elsewhere. Unless British Columbia can meet the price of other parts of Canada, I presume it will be difficult for them to get a contract.
Then, Mr. Shaw, chairman of the supplies board, gave evidence some time ago before the committee on agriculture. Among other things he said this:
We were aware of the plant in question and had it inspected by a dehydration man whose report stated that it was fairly -well equipped but lacked certain equipment for the completion of the dehydration processing of vegetables.
In other words, the report he has given to the committee is to the effect that it is not fully equipped. Then he continued:
Now, that means just what I said in the beginning, that this plant is not at the moment in a complete position to do this job. I stated it would probably be possible, that -we had no objections, in regard to giving a contract if the products were required, providing they gave assurance on two things: First, that they can do this job to the satisfaction of the board, and second, that by doing it at that particular point they do not endanger or short the domestic supply situation.
That is the question just raised by the hon. member for New Westminster, the question as to whether the preparing of dehydrated potatoes in that particular area would short the supplies for cities like Vancouver and Victoria, and for camps out there connected with military operations. Then he continued:
Those are the two conditions and they are very important ones. They are the only points in question. I might mention this, that there are no controls in that plant. Dehydration cannot be conducted without controls, and there has been no application, as far as I am aware, for controls.
In other words, the contention is that the plant is not fully equipped, and that those who are operating would have to satisfy the board that it would be equipped before an order would be given. In the second place, there would have to be satisfactory evidence that there were sufficient potatoes-not five years ago or six years ago, or even last year- but that there would be sufficient potatoes this year to warrant the board's going in there and buying potatoes to be dehydrated for shipment out, when there may have to be potatoes shipped in to feed the people in that area.
If that can be proved satisfactorily, then there is no reason why a contract should not be given. That matter, I believe, has been referred to the wartime prices and trade board, and I understand they have stated- and I presume they had evidence before making the statement'-that while it is true that British Columbia has been exporting potatoes, that very much larger quantities are imported from points outside the province. Considerable quantities move from interior points, such as Ashcroft and Kamloops. The wartime prices and trade board state it is their opinion that a dehydration programme

War Appropriation-Agriculture
at the coast would accentuate this movement which, under war-time conditions, would not appear to be justified. That is their decision on the information they have, up to the moment. They point out that there are so many potatoes being used there that there is some question as to whether we should _ dehydrate potatoes in British Columbia.

I do not know whether I can answer all the statements made by the minister, but certainly I shall answer as many of them as I can remember.
First of all, with regard to the quantity of potatoes may I say that this is not the first occasion I have protested to the Minister of National Revenue against allowing potatoes to enter British Columbia from southern points, at times when the farmers had their pits full of potatoes. The fact that there have been importations of potatoes does not mean that there are no potatoes in British Columbia. We must remember that in some parts of California three crops are grown in a year, on irrigated ground, and that they have cheaper labour. They have sent the surplus crop from California, Oregon and Washington into British Columbia, while our potatoes rotted. I have protested many times in the house about that situation.
At the outset of his remarks the minister stated that whoever had surveyed the plant had said that the equipment this man had was all right for potatoes, but that he did not think it would be satisfactory for vegetables. Let us have a clear picture of this. Just what do they want? Here is an instance where the farmers have made an agreement with the manager of a plant to the effect that they will sell their potatoes to this plant. If they get an ordinary crop of potatoes in British Columbia they will have a surplus this year. I contend that that point has not been investigated. All we are getting now from the minister is a statement that some official says that some things have to be decided to find out whether they will make a contract with the farmers. This is the first part of July; the crop is almost ready for market-. Steps should have been taken long ago. This matter should have been settled months and months ago.
That was the stand taken by the chairman of this firm. Will the minister say on his responsibility as Minister of Agriculture that this is a deficiency area? Will he make a statement now?

The hon. member wants me to make a statement now, and I will. He knows the reason for the action that was taken

last spring as well as I do. He knows of the telegram that we received which threatened not to feed the people of the west coast area.
That has nothing to do with its being a deficiency area. I would take the minister up on that statement if I had time.

That is why potatoes were shipped in. A certain organization in British Columbia threatened this government and threatened the board that they would not even supply potatoes for the military camps, and potatoes were admitted into that area. I do not want to get into any unnecessary discussion about this.
I do not care whether the minister does or not.
That is quite all right. While he was speaking, on at least two occasions, my hon. friend made a statement which I had not given a moment ago.
What were they?
I did not say anything about vegetables and potatoes. I read what I said and I still have it in front of me. That statement can still be read.

The minister is taking another argument. We were talking about dehydrating potatoes at this plant. We were talking about 1943, and the minister is talking about the 1942 crop and what occurred in connection with the potato board of British Columbia. That is an entirely different subject. We realize that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) takes care of the wartime prices and trade board, but I do not want the minister to try to sidetrack the issue.
We were talking about potatoes; we were not talking about vegetables.

If you will read the record you will find that you mentioned that this man said that they had a plant fit to dehydrate potatoes but that it was not fit for vegetables. That was the statement you made. I ask you to read Hansard to-morrow, and you will find you said that in spite of what you say now. I want to know what you are going to do. You have not yet said that there is a deficiency area in British Columbia.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I ask the hon. member for New Westminster kindly to address the Chair.

I will turn and look at you, Mr. Chairman, and perhaps I will not feel as bad.

War Appropriation-Agriculture

If my hon. friend will just permit me, I will read what was said. It reads:
If the Haney plant can be fully and properly equipped for the dehydration of potatoes and can manufacture a product which will meet the board's specifications and if the wartime prices and trade board will approve of the production of additional dehydrated potatoes in British Columbia, the board could give the Haney plant a contract for a small quantity of dehydrated potatoes in 1943 (possibly 200 tons).

We will get the record straight because I am not letting the Minister of Agriculture get away with that. I did not say that that was the statement he referred to. I said that the official he spoke about who investigated the situation had given it as his opinion that this plant had the equipment to dehj'drate potatoes but that they did not have sufficient equipment for vegetables. That was the statement to which I took exception, but now the minister has changed it and gone on to another statement and I am not going to let him do that. I was referring to the official who had investigated this plant, not to the statement which the minister has just read.
I read all of it and there is not a word about vegetables.

Will you go back to the one by the official who investigated the plant? I want to know if there is to be a further investigation and I want to know if the minister is going to see that this plant gets fair treatment.
I have answered that on three occasions and I will answer it again. "If the Haney plant can be fully and properly equipped"-that is the first thing they have to do.
To whose satisfaction?

To the satisfaction of those who are going to buy their product; that is always the person who must be satisfied. "For the dehydration of potatoes and can manufacture a product which will meet the board's specifications"-they have to be properly equipped before they can manufacture that product. "And if the wartime prices and trade board will approve the production of additional dehydrated potatoes"

that raises the question as to whether or not there are sufficient potatoes to supply that particular area. If there are not, there will not be any taken out of the area. If there are sufficient, then they are quite prepared to have potatoes dehydrated. "The board could give the Haney plant a contract for a small quantity of dehydrated potatoes in 1943, possibly two hundred tons." I do not know how I can make the statement any clearer than that.

I am very glad the minister did not reiterate the statement that it was a deficiency area. I should like to know what official of the department advised the wartime prices and trade board that the potatoes of the Fraser valley were not good for eating purposes. Would the minister tell us who that official was? That is a slur on the potatoes of the Fraser valley and something we are not going to let go by just as easy as that. I am addressing you, Mr. Chairman.
I do not know where the hon. member is getting that statement. I cannot find it in anything I have read.
I will produce it later.

I realize that I slowed up the proceedings by raising the question of dehydration, but I had no idea that I was going to start a family quarrel. I may have misunderstood the minister, but from what he said I understood that he would make a general statement on what his department was doing to encourage the dehydration of vegetables and fruits to meet the needs of the war situation. We all realize the desirability of maintaining as good a supply as possible of vegetables and fruits to maintain the health of our people. On account of the difficulties in connection with getting sugar it has not been possible to get canned goods as readily as was the case before the war. My information is that it would be possible to make up that dsficiency to some extent by increasing the commercial dehydration of vegetables and fruits and also encouraging the home hydration of vegetables and fruits. What is the minister's department doing along these two lines?

The dehydrating of vegetables including potatoes was not carried on in any extensive way until a year ago. When the war first began we had been carrying on experiments in dehydration at different farms, more particularly at Kentville, Nova Scotia, and at Summerland, British Columbia. I think it was in the spring of 1941 when some inquiries were made as to whether we could provide dehydrated vegetables, fruits and potatoes to the British food ministry. I think that inquiry was made to the Department of Trade and Commerce through its officials. The officials who were dealing with it at the time were not fully familiar with what was being done in agriculture, but later on in the season the British representatives made representations to the Department of Agriculture, and we were able to satisfy them at that time that we had methods of dehydration which, if applied to some plants in Canada, might produce an

TFar Appropriation-Agriculture
acceptable product. The British representatives made some suggestions as to what equipment might be put in, and those suggestions were added to by the dehydration officials of our different farms.
One of these men has been placed in charge of dehydration in Canada, and there has been the development of plants which was agreed upon between the British government and ourselves. The result is that we have some eight plants operating across Canada. These plants have had some assistance from the government, largely in the matter of how they should be equipped and some assistance in connection with getting the equipment and having it put in the plants. My understanding is that the government is not actually paying out cash, that the equipment is to be paid for by the plants themselves. As I say, some eight or possibly nine plants by now are operating in different places across Canada. They have been providing all the products for which we could get an outlet in our arrangement with the British government. I may say that a year ago, after we got the plants operating, we were not at all certain that we would get rid of all the dehydrated products we had at that time, but since that time satisfactory arrangements have been made and the British are taking these products.

I should like to press further the local aspect of the matter. Is the department doing anything to increase the supply of dehydrated fruits to be avaiable in the home market to replace the canned fruits which are practically off the shelves of Canadian stores?

Ever since the beginning of the war we have had a contract with the Nova Scotia apple people under which apples were dehydrated and also canned. The government has taken delivery of a very considerable part of the apple crop and we have either canned or dehydrated the apples. During the first year of the war we actually gave away a considerable part of the dehydrated product to the British as part of our programme to help out in the marketing of a crop which in those days was not needed; that is, in the form of fresh apples. Since that time we have been encouraging housewives to can fruit and vegetables. We have put out pamphlets which indicate how this canning can be done most satisfactorily and how fruit and vegetables can be dehydrated in the home. That kind of work is being done constantly by the department right across Canada.

This may have been covered while I have been away for the last

few days, but in view of the fact that there is likely to be a shortage of potatoes in this part of Canada again and the possibility that we may have another large crop of potatoes in western Canada, is the department doing anything to see that our surplus potatoes in the west that may come into existence in the fall are properly stored with a view to shipping them later on to points in Canada where they are needed? The minister will remember as I do that last fall on a good many farms in western Canada there were piles of potatoes that could not be used, and yet, as we know, potatoes can be stored very simply. I have seen potatoes just put into a hole in the ground, and if it were deep enough and dry enough and had a little ventilation the potatoes would come out in the spring in excellent shape. I wonder if the department is contemplating urging farmers to store in such simple fashion any of their surplus potatoes under a sort of guarantee that they would be marketed under some government plan in the spring when they would be needed in those parts of Canada where there is likely to be a shortage.
There is considerable difficulty in determining very long in advance whether there will be a shortage.
It looks very much that way now, with the rain rotting the potatoes.

It is, but I was just going to call my hon. friend's attention to the statement that was read in the house the other evening to the effect that there are now 5.000 cars of potatoes south of the line looking for a market, whereas two weeks ago we were worrying because we were not able to get potatoes. Potatoes are a crop that anyone can grow in his back yard, and we have been urging people to grow what we call victory gardens all across Canada. If they have been responding to the appeals we have been making, it is very difficult for anyone to estimate how many potatoes we shall have this fall. On the other hand, I think it is known to farmers right across Canada how potatoes can be pitted. It has long been the practice to pit potatoes for keeping during the winter. Publications go out from the department that give information to those not properly informed as to how that can be done.
I think one of the big problems in connection with potato marketing is this. With prices under control and the price based on some particular season of the year, the farmer finds that if he keeps his potatoes in the cellar during the winter and has to go down and pick them over in the spring and sacrifice-

War Appropriation-Agriculture
probably half of them in order to get the other half, good potatoes that can go on the market, he hesitates to do so if he is controlled by the price in the fall, particularly if labour is short in the spring, which it usually is. I think some attention will have to be given to encouraging the farmer to keep potatoes during the winter and have them ready for marketing in the spring. Right at the time of the potato shortage here I had a letter from a farmer telling me that he had just taken out one hundred bushels of his potatoes from his cellar and fed them to his pigs. He was complaining of the method that had been set up for moving these potatoes from his farm to where someone wanted them. I can understand the farmer doing that, and so can anyone who has been on the farm and knows how farmers store their potatoes and what a job they have in the spring with them and the labour involved in it. If there is a shortage of labour, and that is very likely in the spring, the farmer will feed the potatoes to the pigs. We do all we can to overcome that, but I am sure hon. members will realize we cannot overcome it all.

I have another question that comes to some extent under the minister's department, but largely perhaps under the Department of Trade and Commerce. Is any attempt being made to solve the problem of the transportation of our wheat to the United States for feed? I ask that deliberately, because on Friday of last week I heard that question asked by the vice-president of the United States. Is there an answer to it? I could not answer it.

The position is this.
We shall have in Canada about 649 million bushels of wheat in store at the end of this month, a carryover from preceding years. It is not all feed wheat, but it is wheat that can be fed. But we have a decided shortage of cars on both sides of the line with which to move the grain. That is on account of the fact that the cars are being used to ship minerals, largely iron, and to handle the output of our war factories.
I should say, too, that up until a few months ago there was an embargo on wheat entering the United States, with the exception of feed wheat, and the percentage of our feed wheat is comparatively low. The Americans have recently removed that embargo, but just removing the embargo did not start the wheat to move. There was a lack of cars and a lack of shipping on the lakes to move it. The officials of the wheat board visited Washington and discussed the matter with government and railway officials there, because, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar says, this matter comes under the Department of Trade and Commerce, and they made an arrangement whereby the United States railways would place all the cars they could at the disposal of the Canadian railways to move grain to the head of the lakes. Every hon. member from the west knows that United States cars have been spotted at the towns all up and down our western railways to move the grain to the head of the lakes. It was supposed, if moved in United States cars, to be moved there to be at the disposal of the Americans who would take it away in United States ships.

Are they buying the
wheat from the wheat board?

They are buying on the market, but I presume most of it would come from the wheat board. They have bid prices of SI on the market and take whatever supplies they can get. The grain is then supposed to move down the lakes on United States ships and in United States cars from United States ports. The Americans want the grain in their eastern states where the shortage chiefly exists. They have sufficient grain in the prairie sections where the grain is grown. The grain has to be shipped down the length of the lakes and reshipped by train to the points where it is required. There has been this difficulty of getting sufficient cars and shipping to move feed wheat or coarse grains in the quantities we would like it to move. They wanted to get 200 million bushels, and we would like to sell them 200 million bushels, but up to date they have moved under 100 million bushels. So that the position is not as we would like to have it. The difficulty is transportation, but the railways and shipping are doing the best they can.
Have the two countries a joint organization to handle it?

Yes, there has been
co-operation.

That is what I was not clear about. Apparently the need for feed is becoming acute in the United States. They are faced apparently with the problem of shipping. I was not clear whether there was cooperation between the two sides of the line, and my impression was that some doubt existed in Washington. I wanted to be clear about that.

There is no reason why that feeling should exist. I have heard a little about the questioning that was done by Mr. Wallace. I was in Chicago about two weeks ago and have also heard the questions

War Appropriation-Agriculture
he was asking and I think his questions were based on what was being said as to conditions on this side of the line. I found that many farmers across the border did not realize that there was as large a wheat surplus as there is in Canada, and consequently they were inclined to increase their own acreage in wheat, whereas we have a very large surplus here. That was one of the reasons why I went to Chicago, to make it apparent to them that the grain is here. There is still the transportation difficulty.

The government should get its information board to do something about this, because there is apparently in the United States a lack of understanding of what this country has, of what it is doing and of what it has done. While this is not under the minister's department, I think every effort should be made to publicize what Canada has done toward furnishing free supplies to Great Britain last year and to the united nations this year, and what we are prepared to do in the way of production and the extent of cooperation which we are prepared to give and have given to the United States and the other allied nations. I feel that this is not understood.
Under what item will the minister be prepared to discuss the question of wool prices?
