speechtext:
We are now on item
5. Freight assistance on western feed grains,

I should like to
have the minister's answer. The question of *wool prices is very important and should be discussed.

The wool board is not
under us, but still the special products board is; I think the best place to discuss it is here.

Under what item
would the minister suggest that we discuss the price of beef?
Under what is called the bacon board; it should be the meat board now.

On this item, freight
assistance on western feed grains to eastern Canada, I think this is a policy of the government which was supported quite widely in western and eastern Canada. Would it be possible to have this freight assistance extended to commercial seed grains? What has happened during the past year is that a great deal of feed grain was shipped to eastern Canada and used for seed, because the additional freight on seed grain placed the price out of line with the price of feed grain, so

that a lot of inferior seed has been sold in eastern Canada this year and a lot of good commercial seed had to be sold in western Canada for feed. That position will be even worse in the coming year, because in a great deal of eastern Canada not so much seed grain will be available this year as there was last year. It will be found that in 1944 large quantities of feed grain shipped to eastern Canada will be used for seed, and seed of inferior quality, when better seed is available and could be used to produce more grain than can be grown from; the inferior grain. Would the government consider paying freight assistance on commercial seed for use in eastern Canada?

The freight policy was associated with an attempt to get food for Britain, and the payment of freight from Fort William east was in the hope that we could get enough western grain moved down into the eastern areas to feed all of the live stock there is on eastern farms. I do not know whether the government would be prepared to accept a policy of free freight on seed as well, coming from Fort William east. It is a new idea; I doubt very much whether it is necessary in order to get the results we desire to get at the present time. I am not sure whether the hon. member for Melfort has in mind seed grain or whether he has in mind alfalfa seed, which is grown in his constituency or in that area.

I had not reference to alfalfa seed; I had reference to oats and barley and commercial coarse grain seed which is produced in large quantities and of good quality in western Canada, and has been shipped in considerable quantities to eastern Canada. My understanding is that that freight fell off this spring because some of the better carloads of feed grain were being used by eastern farmers for seed, rather than pay the additional cost on commercial seed grain of standard quality. The result is that there will not be as .much production in eastern Canada from the inferior seed which has been used. I think the government would be quite justified in paying the freight so as to get better seed for eastern Canada, especially in view of the fact that there is likely to be a considerable shortage in seed grain in eastern Canada during the coming year.

Of course I would not be in a position to prove whether or not grain shipped down under the feed policy has been used for seed, other than to say this, that those who collect the money on the freight are supposed to prove that this grain is used for feed. Hon. members will understand that

Mobilization Act
when oats, for example, get out on to the farm it is difficult for any inspector to follow the shipment and say that these particular oats went into feed and these others went into the ground. Nevertheless payment is only supposed to be made if the grain is being fed. For example, we do not pay if grain is milled for any other purpose than feeding live stock. We pay on that proportion of the wheat which goes into bran and shorts which is fed to live stock, but we do not pay on the other part of the wheat which goes into flour. For the same reason we would not pay, if we knew it, on grain which is going into seed, under the present policy. I doubt very much if the government would be prepared to pay freight on seed grain under present circumstances.
Is this assistance being given to British Columbia as well?
Yes. The arrangement is the same. It starts from Calgary and Edmonton west as from Fort William east.
Has the minister anything to show whether the consumption of grain has increased since the freight assistance has been put into effect?
Oh, yes; the amount we have shipped east has been greatly increased. It is about double.
And west?

West, I would think about the same. The freight assistance amounted up to the end of the fiscal year 1943, in round figures, to the following sums; Ontario, $4,600,000; Quebec, $4,900,000; New Brunswick, $900,000; Nova Scotia, $1,300,000; Prince Edward Island $274,000; British Columbia, $1,218,000; making the total $13,343,000. The total for the fiscal year 1943 is $8,906,000, with an additional $708,000 being paid on wheat at eight cents a bushel.

Item agreed to.
Feeds administrator-
Payment of eight cents per bushel in respect of western wheat used exclusively as feed for live stock, $2,000,000.
Does this apply to feed grain shipped east, or anywhere in Canada?
It applies on the same grain shipped to the same points as the other feed grain, and from the same points; that is, from Fort William east to any point and from Calgary and Edmonton west.
But not to any point within the prairies themselves?
Yes.
Why is this amount eight cents a bushel?
It is the difference between the price which the miller is presumed to get the wheat at, and the ninety cents.
Is any of this $2,000,000 paid to millers who are using the wheat for making into flour? Are they paid on the proportion of the bran and shorts which are made out of wheat?

There is a ceiling on flour, and under that arrangement the miller gets his wheat at a certain price. That price is based on what he paid for wheat in September and October, 1941. But the farmer gets ninety cents a bushel for the wheat, and this puts the wheat for which the farmer gets ninety cents a bushel on a feeding basis eight cents lower than that.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
